deep-tech-99adf0b33f.headline: China’s AI models, led by Kimi, dominate open-source enterprise spending
deep-tech-99adf0b33f.fulltext:

Chinese artificial intelligence models led by Moonshot AI’s Kimi family accounted for nearly nine-tenths of estimated global enterprise spending on open-source systems, according to a new study, even though proprietary US rivals continue to capture the vast majority of overall revenue.
The report, released this week by Silicon Valley venture capital firm Menlo Ventures, said Chinese AI systems accounted for 89 per cent of global enterprise spending on open-source models. Kimi led with a 61 per cent share, followed by DeepSeek at 15 per cent and Z.ai’s GLM series at 11 per cent.
By contrast, Meta Platforms’ Llama series, the leading Western offering in the category, accounted for just 7 per cent of open-source enterprise spending.
The global numbers were extrapolated from a September survey of nearly 400 US enterprise decision-makers managing more than US$4 billion in total AI budgets, alongside public filings and third-party reports, according to Menlo.
Unlike closed systems, open-weight models allow developers to download and adapt the underlying parameters rather than access them exclusively via hosted cloud services. Menlo groups such open-weight architectures under the broad label of “open-source”.
Despite the growing adoption of open Chinese architectures, proprietary systems still captured an overwhelming majority of model budgets.
US firms Anthropic and OpenAI commanded a combined 86 per cent of enterprise spending on AI models that were accessed via application programming interfaces (APIs), capturing 55 per cent and 31 per cent respectively, while Google held 9 per cent, the report showed.
In contrast, open-source models represented just 4 per cent of expenditure, even though they accounted for 19 per cent of enterprise usage of tokens – the processing units of AI data.
On global AI model aggregation platform OpenRouter, Chinese models’ token usage exceeded that of US models for the 27th consecutive week from October 26 to November 1.
The dynamic underscores an emerging division across the global AI supply chain: US giants lead in monetising closed-source APIs, while Chinese open models serve as foundations upon which overseas developers adapt to build their own services.
One example is US-based AI coding platform Cursor. In a technical report published in March, Cursor disclosed that its Composer 2 model was built on Moonshot’s Kimi K2.5. The US company refined the Chinese model on code-heavy data sets before applying reinforcement learning to improve its performance in software engineering.
In the report, Menlo said that coding tools and enterprise chatbots now made up 76 per cent of the US$77.3 billion global enterprise AI application market, with autonomous agents driving the next phase of business demand.
Menlo is an active investor in Anthropic, as well as several AI infrastructure providers examined in the report.
Minxiao is a technology reporter at the South China Morning Post, covering semiconductors, AI, and fintech. She previously reported for 36Kr and Harvard Business Review China, specializing in the intersection of AI and emerging technologies. Her coverage focuses on global supply chains, Web3, and RWA.

ai-76a37a2b42.fulltext:
Anthropic pushes ahead with pre-Thanksgiving IPO despite tech selloff, accepts lower valuation
Anthropic is pressing ahead with its IPO despite the tech selloff, accepting a lower valuation. The Claude developer wants to go public before Thanksgiving and raise $80–100 billion at a $1.25–1.75 trillion valuation, according to investors cited by the Financial Times. That tops the current $965 billion but falls short of the $2 trillion the most optimistic investors had hoped for. Annualized reported revenue now sits at about $81 billion, up from roughly $65 billion at the end of July.
Rising borrowing costs and heavy AI spending plans triggered a tech selloff this week. Democrats winning the US midterms accelerated it because they had promised to slow data center construction, including other measures. The Nasdaq 100 dropped 6.4 percent on Thursday but recovered somewhat on Friday.
OpenAI also cut its funding-round target from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion and recently raised only about a third of the $30 billion it originally sought.

indian-startups-dde723e27a.headline: TRAI Backs Direct-To-Device Satellite Connectivity, Proposes New Authorisation Framework
indian-startups-dde723e27a.fulltext: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services using satellite and terrestrial mobile spectrum. The proposals can enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites, potentially extending connectivity to areas without conventional mobile coverage. Under the proposed Satellite Communication Network (SCN) Provider Authorisation, companies can build and operate satellite networks and sell capacity to eligible telecom service providers. They cannot serve end users directly under this authorisation. The recommendations require government approval and do not immediately permit commercial D2D services. What Changes For Operators? The framework would give telecom operators a way to access satellite infrastructure through partnerships, while continuing to manage their customer relationships. For satcom companies, it would create a separate route to sell network capacity to telecom operators, without requiring them to build a consumer-facing service under the same authorisation. In effect, one company can operate the underlying satellite network while another sells connectivity to customers. This will support partnerships between satellite infrastructure providers and telecom operators seeking to extend their coverage. However, the SCN authorisation alone would not allow a satellite company to sell mobile or broadband services directly to consumers. It would require the relevant service licence or authorisation. The proposed nationwide authorisation would remain valid for up to 20 years, with renewal permitted for another period of up to 20 years. Connecting Phones To Satellites TRAI has proposed two routes for D2D connectivity – using spectrum earmarked for mobile satellite services or using spectrum already assigned to terrestrial mobile operators. For the first route, it has recommended that the government encourage handset manufacturers to include support for the relevant satellite bands in future smartphones sold in India. For the second, telecom operators can partner with satellite network providers to use their existing mobile spectrum for satellite connectivity. However, participating operators would collectively need to hold the relevant frequency channel across all 22 licensed service areas and agree to its use. TRAI has recommended permitting this arrangement without waiting for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027. The satellite services would have to avoid interfering with existing authorised services and cannot claim protection from interference caused by them. TRAI has proposed an authorisation fee of 8% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), without a minimum authorisation fee. Satellite network providers can obtain spectrum directly from the government or use spectrum held by eligible partner operators. In a partnership, spectrum rights would remain with the operator. Government-assigned satellite spectrum would be valid for up to five years, with a possible extension of up to two years. It would attract an annual minimum spectrum charge of ₹3,500 per MHz. For D2D services using a telecom operator’s existing mobile spectrum, TRAI has proposed no additional spectrum charges. Existing spectrum charges would continue. The proposals come amid efforts by Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance Jio to tap India’s satellite connectivity market.

OpenAI lands an $11 billion funding round, but has to court dentists for more capital
OpenAI has received roughly $11 billion in new funding, the first tranche of a round valuing the company at $1.25 trillion. The money was wired on Friday, Bloomberg reports. The full round could grow to $20 billion, with the rest expected in the coming weeks. OpenAI originally sought $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation but scaled back after an AI-sector selloff. Anthropic's valuation is also under pressure ahead of its planned IPO.
Investors include Coatue Management, T. Rowe Price, SoftBank, Sequoia Capital, Founders Fund, Andreessen Horowitz, and a consortium from the United Arab Emirates. OpenAI is also working with investment banks to bring in wealthy individual investors. If OpenAI is already courting dentists to scrape together more capital, it tells you the AI funding market is either tapped out or too concentrated on OpenAI and Anthropic. Anthropic's massive B2B success with Claude Code is making life even harder for OpenAI.

climate-energy-ded895ffb9.headline: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December
climate-energy-ded895ffb9.fulltext:
‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December
The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “state of the climate” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets.
Dr Zeke Hausfather, Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ask me anything” session.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.
This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.
The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.
Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.
Writing on CB Connect on 5 November, Hausfather wrote:
“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”
This year’s El Niño has already chalked up a number of milestones.
On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.
Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.

Support award-winning climate journalism
Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.
Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” analysis indicates that El Niño is set to continue to intensify into December, with 10 out of 14 models expecting temperatures in the Niño3.4 region to peak in the final month of this year. The remainder anticipate a November peak.
While human emissions of greenhouse gases are responsible for almost all of long-term global warming, temperatures in specific years are strongly influenced by El Niño events.
The “state of the climate” analysis explains that this year’s El Niño event will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. This is because global temperatures typically lag warming in the tropical Pacific by around three months.
Carbon Brief projects that the 2027 average global temperature will reach around 1.74C above pre-industrial levels. It calculates a 96% chance that next year will be the warmest on record.
This projection is based on the historical relationship between year-on-year temperature changes and El Niño conditions the preceding autumn. It also factors in uncertainty around how global temperatures will develop across the remainder of 2026.

world-c58085b689.headline: Israel’s president picks Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to form government
world-c58085b689.fulltext:
Israel’s president has chosen Gadi Eisenkot, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s strongest rival, to try to form a new government, after a deadlocked election that left neither man with a clear path to power.
Isaac Herzog’s office said he had informed Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, on Saturday night “of his intention to task him with forming a government”.
It added that the formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony on Sunday at the president’s residence in Jerusalem.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot wrote on X in his first reaction to the announcement of his designation.
Netanyahu is fighting to hold on to office after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an election on 27 October but still emerged as the largest bloc in parliament.
Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.
During party consultations with Herzog, 66-year-old Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.
But it remains unclear if Eisenkot’s bloc would accept support from the Arab lists in forming a government.
Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.
He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.
But the military man is no peacenik. He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.
Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by the Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.
After his appointment, Eisenkot will have 28 days to come up with the 61 votes needed for a government. If he comes up short, Herzog can provide a 14-day extension before he has to offer the mandate to someone else.
If neither side succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections. The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 due to repeated deadlocks.

deep-tech-d9c54b5db0.headline: CesiumAstro Raises $730M, Reaches Valuation Above $4.5B
deep-tech-d9c54b5db0.fulltext:
MERRITT ISLAND, FL—CesiumAstro plans to build and deploy a new constellation—called Synchronicity—consisting of 737 satellites. The company made a downpayment on it Thursday, closing a $730M financing round.
Janus Henderson led the equity round, which included additional participation from Insight Partners, Sands Capital, Sumitomo Corporation of Americas, Woven Capital, Incharge Capital, Magnetar, AV, and NewSpace Capital.
The round included a $100M debt facility provided by the Export-Import Bank of the United States and JPMorgan in addition to $630M in equity financing.
Small step, giant leap: The announcement comes just over a month after CesiumAstro sent its first satellite to orbit. Element-1 launched on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare in October, on a mission designed to pave the way for the full Synchronicity constellation.
“You can build a satellite like you used to that’s a billion dollars and bullet proof, but you’ve taken a decade to test it out,” CesiumAstro founder and CEO Shey Sabripour told Payload. “We did [this satellite] in two and a half years.”
Element-1 is the first of eight planned spacecraft with launches secured between 2028 and 2029. These sats are intended to build out CesiumAstro’s in-space compute capabilities.
The proposed Synchronicity fleet is designed to broadcast over Ku-, Ka-, and V-band frequencies, and will come equipped with onboard compute capabilities to deliver competitive flexibility and resiliency for commercial and national security customers.
How the hundreds of Synchronicity sats will get to orbit, however, is an open question. Sabripour said CesiumAstro is strategizing about what partnerships are necessary to reach its goal of 350 satellites in orbit by 2032.
All for one: The constellation will combine tech that CesiumAstro has spent nearly a decade building, through in-house R&D and a slew of recent acquisitions.
In the past year, CesiumAstro purchased three companies, each adding critical IP to CesiumAstro’s portfolio.
- Jariet Technologies, an RF System-on-Chip semiconductor company focused on satcom, electronic warfare, and radar tech. The acquisition added “advanced mixed-signal semiconductors, digital signal processing, and digital beamforming capabilities” to Cesium’s arsenal, according to the announcement.
- 1Aardvark, a mission software company, giving Cesium spacecraft the ability to operate “in contested or connectivity-constrained environments.”
- Vidrovr, an AI company focused on signal analysis, accelerating CesiumAstro’s integration of AI into its satcom operations.
And CesiumAstro doesn’t plan on stopping the shopping spree anytime soon.
“There’s a few things that we’re still buying and will continue to buy if the supply chain is resilient and made in the US,” Sabripour said. “If it’s not, and it’s being endangered because there are a lot of acquisitions then we’ll buy them. We have our eyes on quite a few.”
In addition to more potential M&A opportunities, CesiumAstro plans to use the new funds to invest heavily in its manufacturing capacity—announcing plans to spent $500M over the next five years to expand its footprint in Austin and purchase 270,000 sq ft of manufacturing space.
Although the company’s acquisitions have brought on hundreds of new employees since the buying spree began in February, it plans to add 550 more jobs by 2030.

ai-bc48d8fe5d.headline: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
ai-bc48d8fe5d.fulltext:
AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds
AI models can often spot problematic behavior by other AI agents in logs. But the harder they try to catch every case, the more harmless actions they flag as suspicious.
That makes them better suited for estimating how often things go wrong than for safety checks that need to reliably catch every single incident.
In a post on his Substack "Free Systems," Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views.
Hall replicated and extended a study by the research organization METR. METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash.
The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of reward hacking cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half.
In sandbagging, a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs.
Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did.
Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug.
Newer models barely reduce false alarms
Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs.
GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either.
When auditors are tuned to an 80 percent detection rate, the best models reach false-alarm rates of 2.5 to 3 percent on both reward hacking and sandbagging. Some models do far worse: to catch 80 percent of reward-hacking cases, Opus 4.8 flagged 40 percent and Gemini 3.8 Flash flagged 63 percent of harmless logs as suspicious.
In Hall's worked example with 100,000 agent sessions per month, a 3 percent false-alarm rate would produce nearly 3,000 false warnings against roughly 2,000 real hits. He fears human reviewers facing such stacks would eventually go numb and wave through genuine cases.
A second test using the R-Judge dataset from Shanghai Jiao Tong University shows a similar trade-off for everyday agent tasks. At 5 percent false alarms, Opus 4.8 caught almost 96 percent of unsafe actions. When auditors need to find 95 percent, nearly all models stay below 10 percent false alarms, with Gemini 3.8 Flash even under 4 percent. But when the required detection rate jumps to 99 percent, the false-alarm rate climbs to 15 percent even for the best model, GPT-6 Astra. Gemini 3.8 Flash—the leader at the 95 percent threshold—then flagged 81 percent of safe actions as unsafe.
Large agent incidents overwhelm manual review
The Hugging Face incident shows how pressing the question is. A swarm of OpenAI agents left behind roughly 1,300 transcripts and 1.2 million file fragments. METR analyzed the data largely with AI agents, spending API credits worth about $400,000. The analysis used GPT-5.6 Sol, among other models, which, as previously reported, was itself one of the models involved in the incident.
METR acknowledged that the model often uncritically adopted the perspective of the agents it was examining and that the investigation was not robust against potential deception by the analysis agents. METR has since called for serious incidents to be investigated systematically and as independently as possible.
Whether AI auditors go easy on their own maker's models is still open
Hall's study has its own limits. It is a pilot. For comparability, he kept METR's original prompt largely unchanged; Fable 5 and Opus 5 refused to run the evaluation entirely under that prompt. The reward-hacking numbers rest on just 47 cases, so a single case shifts the rate by about two percentage points. Whether models evaluate agents from the same maker fairly is something Hall says he still wants to investigate.
He calls for auditor models with far fewer false alarms. He also says it needs to be clarified who bears responsibility for which kinds of agent misbehavior. Hall discusses a proposal to give users more control over their own AI auditors.
Some of that is already possible, he notes: coding agents like Codex and Claude Code let users specify that certain actions can run without asking for approval. Anyone who grants such permissions should, in return, bear more responsibility for the consequences. A world where AI can only be checked by other AI would be strange and could get expensive, Hall writes.

A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports.
The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo, which was reportedly based on U.S. intelligence. An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers.
A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”

deep-tech-6d0e914200.headline: AST SpaceMobile To Build New Blacklift Rocket
deep-tech-6d0e914200.fulltext:
Amid a growing launch crunch, AST SpaceMobile ($ASTS) is building its own ride to space.
On Friday, the company announced it is building Blacklift, a 20-ton rocket designed to launch its BlueBird D2D satcom constellation to LEO.
“The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry,” Abel Avellan, AST SpaceMobile’s founder, chairman, and CEO said in a statement.
Rocket details: Blackliftis targeting a first flight in late 2028—an incredibly aggressive timeline to get a new launch vehicle up and running. Until then, it will continue to rely on external launch providers.
The rocket will be powered by Firefly Aerospace’s Miranda and Vira engines.
- Firefly will sell AST SpaceMobile 36 engines for the first three rockets under a $1.3B contract.
- Firefly will also provide engineering support for three years.
- After that, AST SpaceMobile will buy the license to build both engines itself at a new planned manufacturing facility.
Owning the ride: The new rocket could potentially benefit AST SpaceMobile in the battle of the broadbands, especially as access to commercial launch becomes more constrained with the expected end of SpaceX’s commercial Falcon 9 and rideshare flights.
- SpaceX’s Starlink—a top competitor of AST SpaceMobile’s planned BlueBird constellation—already has in-house access to launch through the company’s Falcon 9 and Starship rockets.
- The addition of Blacklift to AST SpaceMobile’s portfolio levels the playing field—if the rocket can actually be quickly and successfully built.

deep-tech-d3e9fc7e02.headline: Key Space Force satellites can’t talk to each other, likely requiring $1B solution: Sources
deep-tech-d3e9fc7e02.fulltext:
WASHINGTON — The Space Force’s multibillion-dollar effort to build a satellite network that rapidly moves data over high-speed laser links will require an entirely new set of satellites and significant extra funding to connect with other military space systems, Breaking Defense has learned.
In effect, this new group of satellites will serve as translators between different sets of optical waveforms — two or three missile warning/tracking constellations in the short term, and others in the future — in order to ensure multiple systems can talk to each other. That connectivity is a vital part of supporting Trump administration’s Golden Dome missile defense initiative that the network is supposed to help speed into existence, multiple sources said.
The Space Force plans to orbit an “operational prototype” of the Space Data Network Backbone being built by SpaceX by 2027. The large constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) will serve as the data backhaul layer — essentially, the central communications traffic router — of the service’s planned SDN architecture, a space-based network of networks designed to connect sensors to shooters.
The Space Force envisions the SDN as a hybrid constellation comprising military and commercial communications satellites that eventually will be able to share data across missions, including missile warning, tracking and targeting as well as both air- and ground-moving target indication. As a top priority, the SDN will focus on connecting to the Space Development Agency’s (SDA) Tracking Layer satellites for detecting and tracking missiles to be stationed in LEO and Space System Command’s (SSC) similar Resilient Missile Warning and Tracking- Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) birds.
SpaceX won a $2.29 billion contract in May to fast-track development of the SDN Backbone to meet President Donald Trump’s 2028 deadline for implementing Golden Dome. The Space Force has not publicly disclosed how many satellites the backbone will include, but the effort is a restructured version of the earlier MILNET constellation, which a Space Force official said last year would comprise more than 480 satellites.
The SDN Backbone’s central feature is the use of lasers for satellite-to-satellite communications. Laser links, which function via optical communications terminals (OCT) on board satellites, allow the transmission of bigger volumes of data faster and more securely than the radio frequency links carried by traditional communications satellites.
However, SpaceX is using proprietary OCTs on the SDN Backbone satellites, dubbed by the company as “Plasers,” that cannot directly exchange data with those equipping both the SDA and SSC missile warning/tracking satellites, according to multiple industry, former government and current Space Force sources. To complicate matters, these sources said, the OCTs used by SDA and SSC also are incompatible.
To address this lack of connectivity, the Space Force is considering a constellation of 12 to 13 additional satellites that could allow otherwise incompatible OCT payloads to exchange data, two industry sources and one former Space Force official said.
The proposed satellites, known as Space Exchange Points (SEPs) or “translator satellites,” are expected to cost somewhere $12-14 million each, these sources said. That means the satellite project itself would cost north of $100 million, but the sources said that the overall cost of the wider overhaul could reach up to $1 billion — quite the price tag especially at a time the Pentagon is expected to get less funding than it asked for from Congress.
Even aside from the extra costs, however, several sources expressed frustration with the situation with regard to the Space Force’s two new missile warning/tracking constellations, saying it could have been avoided had the Pentagon focused on standardization at an earlier date. Instead, the service is now having to scramble to fix a problem that, the sources emphasized, never needed to happen.
An SSC spokesperson declined to comment on the compatibility of its MEO birds with SDA’s LEO satellites or SpaceX’s Plaser and also declined to comment on the SEP program’s end goals and projected costs. SpaceX did not respond to a detailed inquiry from Breaking Defense.
Different Standards Block Connectivity
The crux of the connectivity problem is that the SpaceX, SDA and SSC OCTs are based on different technical standards governing the precise optical waveforms used, and thus how many gigabits of data per second the laser links can transmit, sources explained.
Part of the reason for the standards mismatch is the decision made some time in 2025 by the Department of the Air Force to flip from using SDA’s Transport Layer of data relay satellites as the SDN backbone to instead relying on SpaceX’s constellation — at the time dubbed MILNET and already in use by the National Reconnaissance Office. By that time, SDA already had been developing both the Transport Layer and the Tracking Layer satellites based on its own open-source OCT standard, a first version of which was published in 2022.
“The optical waveform/terminals on SDA’s Transport Layer and Tracking Layer satellites, which carry the SDA OCT Standard, are not directly compatible with the Plaser waveform,” an SDA official confirmed.
The disconnect between SDA and SSC on OCTs is harder to justify, one former Pentagon official said, given that both developmental programs began at roughly the same time in 2019 — and thus could have worked together to develop compatible OCTs. However, one industry source said, a possible argument for the differences is that SDA has been focused on developing OCTs optimized for its LEO-based satellites, whereas SSC is concentrating on operations in MEO where satellites are farther from the Earth and farther from each other than in LEO.
The Space Force is not unaware of the challenge it faces. G.P. Sandhoo, head of both SDA and the Space Force’s new Missile Warning and Tracking Portfolio Acquisition Executive office, on Oct. 28 told a panel at Silicon Valley Space Week conference in Mountain View, Calif., that his shop will eventually need to figure out how to integrate data from sensors carried by satellites in different orbits, according to an article in Space News.
The SDA official added that “interoperability” between the OCTs for the LEO and MEO missile warning/tracking constellations is currently “being evaluated” by the Space Force.
One solution is simply for the SEP satellites to carry both SDA and SSC standard OCTs, along with software to transmit their data to the SpaceX Plaser and the SDN Backbone satellites.
Another potential solution is for both the LEO and MEO constellations to use a new version of SDA’s optical waveform standard, called v.4.0.0, that potentially could resolve the problem in the future, according to current and former Space Force officials.
That standard was developed in consultation with SSC, the former Space Force official said, and has “two modes:” the first essentially is the same standard SDA is using for “LEO to LEO and LEO to ground” communications; the second would allow LEO to MEO optical data transmission. Thus, it could be used to directly link LEO and MEO missile warning/tracking satellites, and avoid having to add a third OCT payload onto the SEPs.
The SDA official said the version 4 standard “is not yet on contract to be fielded in any SDA Tranches, but is in consideration for Tranche 4.”
Key acronyms in this story
SDN – Space Data Network
LEO – low Earth orbit
MEO – medium Earth orbit
SEP – Space Exchange Point
SDA – Space Development Agency
SSC – Space Systems Command
OCT – Optical Communications Terminal
EST – Enterprise Space Terminal
Translator Sats To The Rescue?
SSC has been working on developing its OCTs, called Enterprise Space Terminals (ESTs), since 2024. At the time, the command described the program as designed “to operationalize a new enterprise waveform designed to communicate in the Beyond Low Earth Orbit (bLEO) regimes,” and estimated it would cost a total of $100 million.
This April, General Atomics and CACI announced they had won Phase 3 awards to develop the EST terminals for “flight hardware” production and demonstration, but provided few other details. And in July, SSC awarded California-based startup K2 Space $22.9 million to host tests of two ESTs on two of its Gravitas satellites.
An SSC spokesperson declined to comment on the technical details of the ESTs, saying only that the “EST payload implements a government owned optical communications standard designed for both long- and short-range communications.”
However, the spokesperson confirmed that prototype ESTs are being designed to equip the future SEP translator satellites
SSC initiated the SEP program on Aug. 13 with awards to five companies worth $12 million each — Amazon LEO for Government, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Rocket Lab and York Space System — to build prototypes. The SEP birds are “specialized spacecraft [that] act as orbital routers, allowing disparate networks and government satellite systems to connect directly” to the SDN backbone, the SSC release said.
To do that, the SSC spokesperson said, the SEP “host vehicles” being built by each of the contractors will be “integrated with” the SDN Backbone — implying that they will be equipped with the SpaceX Plaser — and also will carry the ESTs.
“The five vendors will demonstrate their ability to directly connect their host satellite and associated C2 systems to the existing SDN Backbone architecture; ground-to-ground, ground-to-space, then space-to-space,” the SSC spokesperson added. “Each vendor has their own demonstration schedule and we are planning for demonstrations next calendar year.”
However, the spokesperson declined to comment when specifically asked whether the SEP satellites will be equipped with the Plaser. They also declined to specify whether the government had bought those terminals from SpaceX for the SEP prototypes, or whether each vendor instead was required to do so.
(SpaceX in 2024 said it intended to sell a miniature version of the Plaser to allow third party satellites to connect to Starlink, but it is unclear if any such deals have been made — Muon Space in September 2025 announced a “partnership” to equip its Halo birds with the mini-Plaser but did not specify terms.)
The SSC spokesperson noted that the SEP spacecraft vendors also are working with the EST contractors “to define the interface necessary to host their payloads,” stressing that while the contracts are separate the efforts are complementary.
“Combining these host spacecraft and optical payload elements together, a SEP will allow any external Government system carrying a compatible optical terminal to connect to the SDN Backbone,” the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson did not, however, provide any information about the SEP constellation’s ultimate size, costs and schedule for deployment.
The concept of a translator satellite is not a new idea. SDA in 2022 was working on the idea to allow data from commercial satellites eventually to flow into the Transport Layer. But questions remain about how difficult it will be to implement.
“Reasonable people will disagree on how difficult it is,” one former Space Force official said. “[T]he technical challenges from the hardware side are pretty straightforward. … But there is some networking translation that has to happen in addition to just the hardware configuration.”
In addition, the official said, the SEP satellites as currently designed are not compatible with either SDA’s Tracking Layer satellites or the Transport Layer, which is being transferred to SSC for further development as a separate so-called enclave of the SDN specifically focused on connecting to legacy military platforms such as fighter jets.
Which raises the question of whether yet more development and funds will be needed.

indian-startups-20ed893997.headline: MDR And AI: Inside The Two Acronyms That Could Shape Razorpay’s ₹6,000 Cr IPO
indian-startups-20ed893997.fulltext: In March this year, on the sidelines of Razorpay’s annual flagship event FTX, CEO Harshil Mathur told Inc42 that what mattered most to him was how Razorpay stands in the public markets, and not the fact that it went public. Eight months on, that test now has a rough date as the company sets off on the last leg of its IPO journey. Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed IPO. The fintech major is looking to raise ₹5,000-6,000 Cr through a mix of fresh issue and offer for sale at a valuation of around $5 Bn, with a listing likely between January and March 2027. Axis Capital, Kotak Mahindra Capital, JP Morgan and Citi are the reported bankers. The headline number when it comes to Razorpay’s listing, or for that matter any listing within fintech circles, has been that of valuation.Sources suggest that Razorpay may be looking to list at a $5 Bn valuation, a markdown from the $7.5 Bn valuation that the company commanded in December 2021. But back in 2021, fintech valuations were sky high amidst a pandemic led funding boom that witnessed sharp corrections years down the line. Another fintech major, PhonePe, paused its mega listing in March 2026, with reports suggesting that volatile geopolitical tensions and valuation concerns led the payments company to put its IPO plans on hold. It has since revived them on the back of MDR. Sources told Inc42 in September that PhonePe is targeting a listing between February and March 2027 at a valuation of about $10 Bn. But Razorpay has a different story to tell the public investors as it seeks ₹5,000-6,000 Cr from them. The first part of that story is profit. “When you take out that one-time cost of the reverse flip, Razorpay was profitable — that profitability streak is maintained throughout. We hope the financials will continue to improve from here as a company that’s continuously growing,” Mathur had told Inc42 earlier. In FY25, Razorpay slipped into the red, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs from moving its domicile to India. It did not disclose the size of the loss. The reverse flip tax bill has been reported at about ₹1,245 Cr, or about $150 Mn. A year earlier, in FY24, its payments business had reported a ₹34 Cr profit against a total revenue of ₹2,068 Cr or a net margin of 1.6%. The company claims to lead India’s digital payments processing market in terms of total payments volume and is expanding across Southeast Asia and other geographies, but monetising this scale has always been a problem when it comes to payments companies. The 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) on large UPI payments, due after Diwali, would be the first fee on a bulk of these payments, and it would arrive just ahead of the listing window. How much reaches Razorpay’s bottom line depends on two things: how it negotiates with the banks that receive the fee and the large merchants that pay the MDR. Sources we spoke to suggest that much of the revenue bump that companies like Razorpay will get out of MDR would not boost their topline significantly, but could feed profits strongly because it is a fee on rails that companies have already built. For Razorpay, it’s a boost to its search for the right valuation just in time. MDR on UPI would likely narrow the gap between the company’s sought valuation and its bottomline. It also gives Razorpay a growth story to take to public investors as it heads into the IPO. A Profitable Core Unlike many of its contemporaries eyeing a listing at the scale of Razorpay, the fintech has no major debt overhang and nearly half of the IPO proceeds are expected to be allocated for OFS. Company sources told us that the core online payments business is EBITDA profitable and generating strong cash flows, which is why the company is making bold investments in allied businesses and AI. Sources pointed towards capital allocations “between mature, cash-generating units and high-potential growth bets”, with AI-first products, financial infrastructure and new verticals taking the investment. The company has also given a timeline on profitability. “By the end of FY26, our India business should be solidly profitable. At the consolidated level, we’ll reach profitability about two to three quarters after that,” the company’s CFO, Arpit Chug, told Inc42 in October 2025. But FY26 has since closed, and Razorpay is yet to make those numbers public. The biggest factor in Razorpay’s IPO will be the profitability and the margins earned by its core business. In lieu of actual profit figures, Razorpay’s pitch to public investors rests on scale. It described itself in 2024 as India’s market leader in digital payments processing, with a majority share, and said in 2025 that it served 105 of India’s 119 unicorns. It claims to be processing a total payments volume (TPV) of over $180 Bn (as of 2024 end). When compared against its primary competitors Cashfree and PayU, Razorpay stands out for its scale and its focus on small and medium businesses. Razorpay claims to lead on overall volumes, enterprise accounts drive the bulk of volumes at Cashfree, Inc42 reported earlier. Razorpay, on the other hand, claims that 80% of its client base comprises SMBs and startups. Among the three, PayU India leads in terms of the topline. Its payments business alone earned $523 Mn (about ₹4,420 Cr) in FY25. It pulled ahead of Razorpay which reported ₹3,783 Cr in FY25, while Cashfree stood at ₹640.1 Cr. PayU owner Prosus claims the company has a 25% share of the Indian online payments, while processing $90 Bn in TPV in FY26. In a bid to race past the competition, Razorpay has been eyeing overseas markets by strategic tie-ups and acquisitions. Mathur earlier said that international was its fastest-growing business, with payments growing about 40% and newer segments at 70-90%. Outside India, Razorpay currently operates in Malaysia and Singapore and is eyeing expansion into the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam as its next Southeast Asian targets. The company, according to sources, is expanding majorly within Southeast Asia and expects the revenue from these countries to contribute 15% of its overall topline by 2030. Razorpay entered Malaysia by buying a majority stake in Curlec in 2022, launched its gateway there in 2023 and entered Singapore in March 2025. Closer to home, the biggest expected lever is UPI and the introduction of MDR soon after the festive season. About half of the payments flowing through Razorpay are on UPI, and that rail is about to start earning the fee that can feed the company’s bottomline. The Two Negotiations Behind Razorpay’s MDR Upside The first critical negotiation for Razorpay will be with banks. Payment aggregators such as Razorpay get no fixed share under NPCI’s stated framework, because they are not direct members of the UPI network and are part of it only through sponsor banks. So the aggregator’s cut has to come out of the acquirer bank’s share in the MDR, under a private contract between the two. Reports suggest that the talks have centred on aggregators keeping 50-80% of the acquiring bank’s MDR share. But there is also a flip side to it. Payment aggregators and gateways already earn technology, checkout and reconciliation fees from merchants, and with MDR coming into effect, the merchants can move to the aggregators and gateways that offer more reasonable take rates. Pine Labs CEO Amrish Rau has already flagged that talks with merchants have yielded this view among the primary customer base for payments aggregators. “From a commercial standpoint, I absolutely do believe when it comes to the largest of large merchants that we have with us, there will be a commercial conversation to be had, for sure,” Rau said in October 2026 after the Q2 results. Notwithstanding the restructured commercial agreements that the payment aggregators and gateways will sign with banks and merchants for the MDR regime, sources say that the fee could support higher valuations for IPO-bound companies such as Razorpay and PhonePe. “The headline MDR pool is not the same as revenue accruing to an individual participant. It depends on eligible transaction volumes, merchant mix and the prescribed distribution across the ecosystem,” PhiCommerce CEO Rajesh Londhe told Inc42. Listed peer Paytm has already put a number on what MDR will bring to the table. With its Q2 results, Paytm said it expects an uplift of about 2.5 bps in its overall payments processing margin, and that the actual outcome may stabilise in 2-3 quarters after implementation. As per sources, MDR could bring Razorpay ₹192-461 Cr of revenue a year once implemented, which would be about 5-12% of its FY25 revenue and 15-36% of its FY25 gross profit. As a result, analysts believe that Razorpay could see a valuation bump of $300 Mn-$1 Bn from the existing ask. That’s what the MDR effect can actually unlock, though much would also depend on the commercial agreements with banks and merchant talks. Razorpay’s technology prowess and merchant scale could be a huge lever in any talks with banks and merchants. However, what matters more than the scale will be the value of transactions and the scale of the clients themselves, which would directly boost revenue and improve margins. Nearly 80% of Razorpay’s customers are small businesses, digital-first brands and startups, and it has not disclosed how many of their tickets cross the ₹2,000 threshold required for the MDR boost. There is also no certainty as yet on the timeline by which fintech companies can expect the MDR outcome to start showing up on their P&L. Analysts tracking the industry, however, say that the companies would need a few quarters of data to give investors a credible outlook. For Paytm, that could be 2-3 quarters, and with Razorpay coming to the IPO table, investors would want to hear a number for the company. Will a listing between January and March of 2027 be enough to give investors a clear answer? The AI Story Needs Numbers Then there’s the AI story, which we had written about extensively earlier this year. According to Mathur, Razorpay is building a long-term business bet on AI and this is not related to the IPO and its outcome. The fintech sector has been one of the earliest adopters and partners of frontier AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude, experimenting with AI use cases for the millions of merchants on its platform. Razorpay’s Agent Studio, built on Anthropic’s Claude, offers small businesses task-specific agents for abandoned carts, disputes, subscription recovery and cash flow forecasting. Mathur wants Razorpay to be known as “an operating system for businesses” which is run on AI. That story gives investors a reason to look past the thin margins in the payments business, but the AI theme is not strong enough in the case of Razorpay yet. It has to make a bigger splash in terms of the outcomes it is seeing. . Rivals Cashfree, PayU and Pine Labs are also accelerating their AI led partnerships to offer new products to their existing merchant base. All these AI offerings have been particularly concentrated towards agentic workflows and ecommerce enablement. However, there is still little public evidence of what these agents earn. Mathur earlier told us that it will take a few years to assess the real term monetisation value that these AI capabilities can unlock for any fintech. Hence for an IPO-bound Razorpay, its core payments business is the only true and measurable metric for the public investors. The future bets may fructify but for now, they are unlikely to be a factor for investors. Even at a reported $5 Bn valuation, Razorpay goes to market with some real strengths such as 65% YoY revenue growth in FY25, about $180 Bn in annualised TPV, and a profitable core. While it is banking on the MDR regime to solve a lot of headaches, investors will want to see a lot more to justify the valuation ask. indian-startups-d631a26419.headline: OYO Parent PRISM’s Profit Jumps 17% YoY To ₹353 Cr In Q1
indian-startups-d631a26419.fulltext: IPO-bound hospitality chain PRISM, the parent entity of OYO, reported a consolidated profit after tax (PAT) of ₹353 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 17.3% from ₹301 Cr in the year-ago period. According to PRISM’s audited financials seen by Inc42, the profitability came largely on the back of a deferred tax credit of nearly ₹244 Cr in the quarter under review. Nevertheless, PRISM continued to grow its top line and generated an operating revenue of ₹2,814 Cr in Q1 FY27. This was nearly 35% higher than ₹2,078 Cr reported in the year ago quarter. The IPO-bound startup also managed to improve its EBITDA by 24.3% to ₹760 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹611 Cr in Q1 FY26. On the operational front, PRISM’s gross booking value (GBV) stood at nearly ₹9,600 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026, up nearly 30% from ₹7,408 Cr in Q1 FY26. This is largely in line with what PRISM founder and CEO Ritesh Agarwal had said during the company’s extraordinary general meeting (EGM) in October this year. “Our performance (in Q1 FY27) across segments on hotels or on vacation homes has demonstrated improving gross margins, higher operating earnings, even as we invest in expanding our brands and strengthening customer demand,” Agarwal had said then. During the EGM, Agarwal also attributed PRISM’s performance to investments made in technology, brands and distribution capabilities over the past few years. Founded in 2012 by Agarwal, OYO initially operated a budget hotel chain. It has since grown into a hospitality giant that offers holiday homes, coworking spaces, motels and corporate stays in more than 35 countries. The startup’s parent Oravel Stays rebranded to PRISM last year ahead of its initial public offering (IPO). The startup has raised about $3.5 Bn in funding to date and counts the likes of SoftBank, Lightspeed India, Peak XV Partners and Microsoft among its backers. The Q1 FY27 performance comes as PRISM is gearing up to list on the bourses. The hospitality giant first filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in December last year. It then received the market regulator’s approval for its IPO in June this year. Right after, the startup filed its updated DRHP with SEBI for a ₹6,650 Cr IPO, which will comprise entirely of a fresh issue of shares. The Ritesh Agarwal-led startup is said to be eyeing a valuation of $7 Bn to $8 Bn for the public issue.

indian-startups-912e54654d.headline: MobiKwik To Begin NBFC Operations Within 6 Months Post RBI Clearance
indian-startups-912e54654d.fulltext: MobiKwik’s wholly owned subsidiary, MobiKwik Financial Services Pvt Ltd (MFSPL), has received a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from the RBI to operate as a non-banking financial company (NBFC). The certificate was issued on November 5, following the RBI’s in-principle approval in April 2026. The dedicated NBFC was officially incorporated on March 13, 2025. With the regulatory clearance in place, MFSPL intends to commence operations over the next three to six months. It intends to operate on an asset-light co-lending model, partnering with banks and other NBFCs. In a statement, the company said that it plans to complement its existing lending service provider (LSP) business with the ability to originate credit directly through its NBFC. "This will provide greater flexibility in product development, faster go-to-market execution and opportunities to improve lending economics, while allowing the group to continue leveraging its partnerships with established lenders," the company said. MobiKwik aims to disburse loans worth ₹5,000 Cr over the next three to four years, covering secured and unsecured credit for consumers and MSMEs. Cofounder and CFO Upasana Taku said that the NBFC extension would allow MobiKwik to build on its existing lender partnerships and technology infrastructure while participating more actively in the lending value chain. The company plans to focus on responsible lending, prudent underwriting and sustainable growth. During its Q2 earnings call, the CFO noted that MobiKwik could initially route around 10% of its digital lending disbursals through the NBFC. If the company disburses ₹6,000 Cr through its digital lending business next year, it would aim to route ₹600 Cr through MFSPL. Under a proposed 10:90 co-lending arrangement, MobiKwik would contribute 10% of the loan amount, while its lending partner would fund the remaining 90%. This would require around ₹60 Cr in capital from MobiKwik to support ₹600 Cr in disbursals, allowing it to limit its on-book exposure while leveraging its existing underwriting and collections capabilities. The NBFC launch comes amid an uptick for MobiKwik’s business. MobiKwik reported a consolidated net profit of ₹11.8 Cr in Q2 FY27 against a net loss of ₹28.6 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Operating revenue increased 9.4% YoY to ₹295.7 Cr from ₹270.2 Cr. The company said it recorded its highest-ever quarterly net profit, marking its fourth consecutive profitable quarter. During the quarter, MobiKwik’s financial services business segment, which includes its ZIP EMI credit offering, increased 41.8% YoY to ₹86.9 Cr. Loan disbursals through its lending partners rose 34.1% YoY to ₹1,082.6 Cr, up 46.9% sequentially from ₹736.7 Cr. The sequential recovery followed a temporary dip linked to technology infrastructure migration during the transfer of its lending business. MobiKwik increased its major lending partners to 11 from six a year earlier. It classifies partners with quarterly disbursals exceeding ₹5 Cr as major lenders. Of the total disbursals, 21% came through its distribution model, while the remaining 79% were under its first-loss default guarantee (FLDG) model, under which it shares credit risk with lending partners. Lending-related expenses, including operational and financial guarantee costs, declined 16.4% YoY to ₹29.8 Cr. The company attributed the reduction to improved credit quality and better commercial terms with lending partners. MobiKwik expects lending disbursals to maintain strong double-digit growth as newer partnerships mature and it introduces additional product categories, although management cautioned that the growth rate may moderate. Shares of MobiKwik ended today's trading session 2.3% higher at ₹224.75 apiece on the BSE.

climate-energy-138f583619.headline: Global Science Panel Hits Roadblocks Ahead of COP31 Climate Summit
climate-energy-138f583619.fulltext:
Scientists working on new reports for the IPCC, the U.N.’s climate science panel, warn about a funding crunch and report timelines in an open letter.
As global climate negotiators and government officials convene for the annual United Nations climate summit, the scientific organization they rely on to guide their decisions is mired in gridlock and short on funds.
Since 1990, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has produced influential global reports in cycles. Its 2013 and 2014 reports provided the scientific foundation for the 2015 Paris climate agreement, which continues to shape international climate policy. But the IPCC suspended its mid-October meeting without approving a budget for next year or agreeing on a timetable for publishing upcoming reports.
The political disputes that derailed the meeting rattled many of the scientists who devote hundreds of hours, often without pay, to assess the latest climate research across dozens of disciplines, from ice sheets and glaciers to forests and agriculture. Their work not only tracks the science of a changing climate, it also identifies ways to cut greenhouse gas emissions and helps communities adapt to increasingly severe climate impacts.
We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.
Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.
A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.
Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.
A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.
More than 100 IPCC scientists expressed their concern about the future of the panel in an Oct. 19 open letter, asking political leaders to provide it with adequate resources. The scientists reaffirmed their commitment to the work, but warned that, as climate impacts intensify, governments must ensure the panel can produce timely assessments of climate risks and potential solutions when they are needed. They also called for a process that gives all countries an equitable voice, rather than allowing wealthy, industrialized nations to dominate.
The IPCC will resume its session online in December, after the annual COP, the Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This year’s event, COP31, begins next week in Antalya, Turkey. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change continually informs the negotiations with science updates, but political tensions have affected its budget and timelines for upcoming reports.
Governments decide voluntarily each year how much to contribute to the panel’s annual budget of $9.7 million, about the cost of producing a major movie. That pays to keep the meetings running, covering travel, scientific support and workshops, especially for developing countries.
Next year’s budget remains uncertain, but a concerted push by nations to increase funding at the upcoming climate summit in Turkey could be effective, history shows. In 1999, at COP5, an urgent funding appeal in the meeting’s final decision document helped the IPCC maintain momentum for its third and fourth cycles of updated climate reports.
Repeated reminders from the annual climate COPs helped sustain funding through the early 2010s, leading up to the landmark Fifth Assessment Report that is the scientific basis of the 2015 Paris Agreement, which aims to limit human-caused warming as close to 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5C) as possible.
The United States has, at times, contributed as much as one-third of the IPCC’s annual budget. The Trump administration’s withdrawal of funding over the last two years, along with the U.S. government’s withdrawal from the panel, likely contributed to stalling the IPCC process, said Bob Kopp, a climate scientist and professor at Rutgers University, who signed the Oct. 19 letter and has worked on several of the panel’s reports.
Despite the loss of federal support, the United States still has a significant scientific presence in the current assessment cycle, Kopp said. The U.S. Academic Alliance for the IPCC was formed in 2025 by the American Geophysical Union, bringing together colleges and universities to help ensure continued U.S. scientist participation without federal support. He said the U.S. has the largest percentage of contributing authors of any country, about 7.5 percent, and that the alliance nominated more authors for the current cycle than the U.S. government did for the previous one.
“I’m very pleased that civil society in the U.S. has managed to fill some of this gap,” he said. “But we can also see from what’s happening among the governments and the IPCC budget that there’s only so much civil society can do on its own.”

Key IPCC reports are scheduled to track whether countries are living up to what they promised in the Paris Agreement, said Carl Schleussner, a climate scientist with Climate Analytics and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis. Without a timeline for those reports, scientists can’t plan their IPCC-related work schedule, he said.
The delay in the IPCC’s process reflects a range of complex factors, against a backdrop of deteriorating international cooperation. Among them are concerns raised by a group known as the Like-Minded Developing Countries, including India and China. They are questioning whether the panel’s scenarios fairly represent the range of possible climate pathways for all countries, according to reports by observers with the International Institute for Sustainable Development’s Earth Negotiations Bulletin.
Davide Faranda, another IPCC author who signed the letter, said he’s concerned that a breakdown of international collaboration could lead to climate information being weaponized.
If the IPCC fails to provide that timely, widely available knowledge, major powers like the United States or Russia could try to keep climate assessments private to gain strategic advantages through knowledge of climate impacts on agriculture, natural resources, national security and other sectors, he said.
“I think that everyone is aware that climate change now is hitting the entire world like a hammer … and the consequences are here,” said Faranda, who studies climate extremes at the French National Center for Scientific Research in Paris. “Having a report that is transparent and accepted worldwide is important.”
The delays in IPCC decision-making may also reflect the broader redistribution of power in a volatile world. He said the process “should respect that there are new equilibria” emerging.
“We cannot have the deliberations driven only again by European and British and American scientists,” he said. “We have to make it more inclusive. We have to respect the fact that there are countries that are developing fast, and they need to have a stronger voice also in the IPCC.”
The panel’s overall role may be shifting, added Mike Hulme, a professor of human geography at the University of Cambridge who has studied the IPCC.
In the late 1980s and early 1990s, the IPCC mission was clear, he said: detect if the climate is changing and whether humans are causing the warming. The panel answered those straightforward scientific questions by the mid-1990s. After that, things became more complicated.
The climate crisis, he said, raises deep and fundamental questions about the trajectory of human development on the planet. Today, the IPCC grapples with questions that have significant political implications, including how to address global warming through mitigation, adaptation, geoengineering and carbon removal.
The resulting political tension can slow the IPCC’s work, Hulme said. That tension, he added, is also reflected in questions about the coal-producing status of the current two COP31 host countries, Turkey and Australia, and of previous hosts with economies heavily dependent on fossil fuels.
“These political things are very much in the foreground right now,” Hulme said. “The idea that the IPCC can somehow run through that fire with some sort of fireproof clothing on is a non-starter.”

global-economics-a4e5b28d6d.headline: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as Elon Musk focuses on robotics and AI
global-economics-a4e5b28d6d.fulltext:
Elon Musk has announced that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck, marking the end of a failed effort to take a chunk of the lucrative market for pickups in the US.
The billionaire chief executive said production of the car would stop in about the middle of next year at the company’s factory in Texas in order to use the plant for the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.
Musk did not say whether Tesla had plans to produce the vehicle in another factory, although that would probably require significant investment for the specialised tooling needed to make it.
Musk has pinned hopes for Tesla on robotics, artificial intelligence and an autonomous driving fleet rather than following the traditional carmakers’ approach of developing a steady stream of new models to entice private buyers.
It caps a tricky week for the world’s richest person, after Republican candidates he had backed with $446m (£332m) in donations lost in the US midterm elections. The paper value of Musk’s fortune fell by $113bn after the extent of the rout became clear, as stock market investors questioned whether a Democrat-led Congress could slow the pace of the AI boom.
Tesla shares fell by 11% on Thursday, while his AI and rocket launch company, SpaceX, dropped by 9%.
Tesla started deliveries of the Cybertruck in late 2023, after several long delays as the company tried to cope with the technical challenges of producing such an unusual vehicle – and particularly its steel shell.
The Cybertruck never made it on sale in Europe because it did not reach the required safety standards.
Even before sales began, Musk acknowledged how difficult it would be to make it a success. In a 2023 earnings call, he said: “We dug our own grave with Cybertruck,” and noted “enormous challenges” in increasing production and earning money from it.
Musk had said the company aimed to sell 200,000 Cybertrucks each year but it never approached that target. Tesla does not report sales of the trucks separately but in the third quarter of 2026 it delivered only 8,300 “other models”, which include the Cybertruck. The vast majority of its sales were the Model 3 saloon and the Model Y SUV, with 478,000 combined deliveries during the quarter.
Tesla also this year stopped production of its Model S and Model X, its premium saloon and SUV, amid declining sales for ageing products.
Tesla’s automotive focus has shifted to the Cybercab. Tesla has started offering paid trips in the car, which has space for two passengers and no steering wheel, in limited parts of Austin, Texas. However, it is unclear how quickly the company will be able to roll out the taxi service around the US or further afield amid close regulatory scrutiny of driverless car technology.
As well as the Cybercab, Tesla is still ramping up production of its long-delayed Semi electric lorry. Musk is also aiming to produce one other new model: the Roadster sportscar, which Musk revealed with a demonstration of a “flying car” version that used thrusters developed by SpaceX to drive up a curved ramp before flipping and landing. Tesla is aiming to start production of a road-bound version in 2028. Analysts do not expect the Roadster to make a large difference to Tesla’s future profits.
Beyond vehicles, the Texas factory will also be used to build Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot.
Musk posted on X, the social network he owns: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

world-393e0d6d57.headline: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid
world-393e0d6d57.fulltext:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said.
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

other-interests-90dd8695bd.headline: ‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption
other-interests-90dd8695bd.fulltext:
In early October, the artificial-intelligence firm OpenAI posted more than 700 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts on an online public repository. The arguments — if found to be correct after verification — contain an extraordinary trove of new mathematical knowledge. The reaction to these developments from the maths community has ranged from exhilaration to despair. Some researchers worry they have spent their lifetimes attempting to solve problems and their work might now suddenly seem meaningless. Others have expressed concern about the negative impact on young colleagues who are entering the field during a period of flux. And there’s been widespread anger at the manner in which AI companies are releasing such findings.
As one of the authors of the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics, which was published in June, I think some of the field’s concerns over OpenAI’s approach to announcing its discoveries could have been anticipated. In our declaration, we did not oppose the use of AI but put forwards several practical safeguards. These included the need for clear citation policies, precise disclosures on how AI is used and a renewed commitment to the long-standing expectation that all arguments made in a maths proof should be independently verifiable and answerable by a human author. Some AI companies have agreed to follow the declaration. OpenAI has not.
Mathematicians are developing rules for AI use — other fields should follow
Now that mathematicians have started analysing the AI-assisted proofs, it’s clear that many of the 700 preprints are presented in a sloppy, rough-and-ready style, making them hard to understand. The inner workings of OpenAI’s closed models are unknown, and there is also no human author named who might take responsibility for explaining or correcting the content if flaws emerge. It will take mathematicians a lot of time and effort to check the work in the preprints and rewrite it in a professional format that is suitable for judgement by peer reviewers. Unsurprisingly, many mathematicians are unenthusiastic about clearing up OpenAI’s mess, however exciting the underlying mathematics might be.
So, what does this mean for the future of mathematics? Creatively rethinking how the field must evolve will require action at every level. Outstanding leadership by individuals such as mathematician Terence Tao, and grassroots initiatives such as the Leiden declaration, need to be complemented with high-level engagement from stakeholder institutions such as the International Mathematical Union. It would be a disservice to the field if AI companies are allowed to set the norms on how to do mathematics without wide-ranging input from academics.
